    Frequency, Phase and Synchronisation¶

    Code: Open in Colab · Download the notebook · View on GitHub

    In the previous guide we simulated continuous systems and coupled them on networks. Coupled chaotic systems can move together in surprising ways: their trajectories can become identical, or only their rhythms can lock while their amplitudes stay unrelated. To describe this, we first need to say what the amplitude, the phase and the frequency of a signal are, which is simple for a sine wave but not for a chaotic signal. In this guide, we follow Chapter 4 of the PhD thesis [1] from the sine wave to the Fourier transform, the spectrogram and the analytic signal of Gabor, and then use these tools to study complete and phase synchronisation in networks of 5 nodes and to measure them.

    You will learn:

    1. what the amplitude, the phase and the frequency of a signal are, starting from circular motion;
    2. how the Fourier transform finds the frequencies of a signal, even in noise, and why it fails when the frequency changes in time, where the spectrogram helps;
    3. how the Hilbert transform gives the instantaneous amplitude, phase and frequency of any signal, and when these are meaningful;
    4. what complete synchronisation and phase synchronisation are, with coupled logistic maps and coupled Rössler oscillators;
    5. how to quantify synchronisation with the amplitude order, the Kuramoto phase order and the pairwise phase order.

    1. Amplitude, Phase and Frequency of a Sine Wave¶

    From the point of view of signal processing, the amplitude, the phase and the frequency are the three main characteristics of a signal [1]. They have a clear physical meaning for circular motion. An object moving on a circle of radius \(A\) around the origin is at the angle \(\theta\), its phase, measured from the \(x\)-axis, and the rate of change of the phase is its angular velocity, \(\omega = d\theta/dt\). The projection of its position on the \(y\)-axis is the sine wave

    \[ x(t) = A \sin(2\pi f t), \]

    where \(A\) is the amplitude and \(f\) the frequency, the number of cycles per second; the period \(T = 1/f\) is the duration of one cycle. Since the phase is \(\theta = 2\pi f t\), the frequency and the phase are related by

    \[ \omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt} = 2\pi f \quad \Longrightarrow \quad f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{dt}, \]

    which is Eq. (4.5) of the thesis. We use \(A = 2\) and \(f = 2\), so the wave completes 4 cycles in 2 seconds, as in Fig. 4.5 of the thesis.

    Figure 1: (a) The sine wave \(x(t) = 2\sin(4\pi t)\) for \(t \in [0, 2]\) seconds; the red points mark the maxima, where the phase is \(\pi/2\), \(5\pi/2\), \(9\pi/2\) and \(13\pi/2\). (b) The phase of the signal in \([0, 2\pi)\) as a function of time: the phase \(\theta = 2\pi f t\) inside the sine (blue) and the phase obtained from the Hilbert transform of Section 4 (orange), which is shifted by \(\pi/2\). (c) The circular motion behind the sine wave: an object (red) on a circle of radius 2 at the phase \(\pi/4\).

    The \(\pi/2\) shift in Fig. 1(b) is not an error. As we see in Section 4, the Hilbert transform measures the phase of \(\cos\), so for \(x(t) = A \sin(2\pi f t) = A \cos(2\pi f t - \pi/2)\) it gives \(2\pi f t - \pi/2\) [1, 5]. Both phases grow at the same rate, so they give the same frequency.

    2. The Fourier Transform¶

    To find the frequencies in a signal, we use the Fourier transform (FT) [4, 5]. For a signal in continuous time, it is

    \[ X(f) = \mathcal{F}\{x(t)\} = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\, e^{-2\pi i f t}\, dt , \]

    and for a signal in discrete time, the integral becomes a sum. \(X(f)\) is a complex number for every frequency \(f\), which we can write in polar form,

    \[ X(f) = |X(f)|\, e^{i\theta(f)}, \]

    where \(|X(f)|\) is the Fourier amplitude and \(\theta(f)\) the Fourier phase of the frequency \(f\). The FT is commonly used to identify the dominant frequencies of a signal, to reduce noise and to filter the frequencies of interest. Following Section 4.3.2 of the thesis, we take a signal made of three sine waves,

    \[ x(t) = 0.5\sin(2\pi \cdot 10\, t) + 0.7\sin(2\pi \cdot 20\, t) + \sin(2\pi \cdot 30\, t), \]

    and the noisy signal \(x_s(t) = x(t) + \gamma\), where \(\gamma \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 4)\) is Gaussian noise with variance 4, much larger than the signal itself. We sample both at 1000 points per second for 1 second. For a sampled signal of \(N\) points, \(2|X(f)|/N\) gives the amplitude of the sine wave at frequency \(f\).

    Amplitudes recovered from the noisy signal at 10, 20, 30 Hz: [0.4  0.72 1.09]

    Figure 2: (a) The signal \(x(t)\), made of three sine waves, and (b) its Fourier amplitude, with peaks at 10, 20 and 30 Hz of heights 0.5, 0.7 and 1. (c) The noisy signal \(x_s(t)\), in which the sine waves can no longer be seen, and (d) its Fourier amplitude, where the three peaks still stand out.

    Despite the strong noise, the dominant frequencies of the noisy signal are those of the original one, and their amplitudes, 0.40, 0.72 and 1.09, are near the true values 0.5, 0.7 and 1; the noise adds only small peaks at the other frequencies. This is why the FT can be used to remove noise: keeping only the dominant frequencies and transforming back gives the original signal.

    3. The Spectrogram and Signals whose Frequency Changes¶

    The FT assumes that every frequency is present over the whole signal. Signals whose statistical properties, such as the mean and the variance, stay the same in time are called stationary; a composite of sine waves with constant frequencies is an example. When the frequency changes in time, the signal is nonstationary, and the FT cannot show the change. In that case, we compute the FT in a window that slides along the signal, which gives the spectrogram: the power \(|X(f)|^2\) of every frequency as a function of time.

    Following Section 4.3.2 of the thesis, we take the signal

    \[ x(t) = 0.5 \sin\big(2\pi \cdot (0.5\,t)\, t\big) = 0.5\sin(\pi t^2), \qquad t \in [0, 10], \]

    sampled at 100 points per second. Note that the frequency of this signal is not the \(0.5\,t\) written inside the sine: its phase is \(\theta(t) = \pi t^2\), so by Eq. (4.5) its frequency is \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{dt} = t\) Hz, which grows from 0 to 10 Hz. For the spectrogram, we use windows of 100 points, as in the thesis. In the last panel, we also show the instantaneous frequency computed with the Hilbert transform of the next section.

    Figure 3: (a) The signal \(x(t) = 0.5\sin(\pi t^2)\), whose frequency grows linearly in time. (b) Its Fourier amplitude, spread over all frequencies from 0 to 10 Hz with no dominant one. (c) Its spectrogram, the power of the FT in sliding windows of 100 points in decibels, where the bright band of the dominant frequency rises linearly in time. (d) The instantaneous frequency from the Hilbert transform and Eq. (4.5) (blue), which follows the exact frequency \(f = t\) (black dashed), with small oscillations towards the end, where the abrupt end of the signal disturbs the Hilbert transform.

    The FT of the whole signal in Fig. 3(b) tells us which frequencies occur, but not when. The spectrogram and the instantaneous frequency recover how the frequency changes in time.

    Regular and chaotic signals¶

    We now apply the FT to two signals of the logistic map, as in Section 4.3.2.1 of the thesis: a periodic orbit of period 4 at \(r = 3.5\) and a chaotic orbit at \(r = 4\). As in the thesis, we assume a sampling rate of 100 Hz, i.e. one iteration every 0.01 seconds, and use \(10^4\) points. We subtract the mean of each signal first, so that the FT does not show a large peak at \(f = 0\).

    Figure 4: (a) The periodic orbit of the logistic map at \(r = 3.5\), which repeats every 4 points, and (b) its Fourier amplitude, with only two peaks, at 25 Hz and 50 Hz. (c) The chaotic orbit at \(r = 4\) and (d) its Fourier amplitude, spread over all frequencies with no dominant one.

    With a sampling rate of 100 Hz, a pattern that repeats every 4 points repeats 25 times per second, hence the peak at 25 Hz in Fig. 4(b). The larger peak at 50 Hz, the highest frequency that a sampling rate of 100 Hz can show, comes from the alternation of high and low values at every step, which is visible in Fig. 4(a). The periodic signal is thus fully described by two frequencies, while the chaotic signal has no dominant frequency, which is why we need a different notion of phase and frequency for chaotic signals.

    4. The Analytic Signal and the Hilbert Transform¶

    For a periodic motion, the frequency is the number of cycles per unit of time. For nonstationary and chaotic signals, the amplitude, the phase and the frequency have no such clear physical meaning, and they are not uniquely defined [7, 8, 9, 10]. Still, it is useful to define them for every point in time, which is why they are called instantaneous. For example, the phase of systems whose attractor turns around a centre can be defined with a Poincaré section [3], but this does not work for every signal, and the empirical mode decomposition of [9] splits a signal into components with a meaningful phase, but the components are not unique. In this library, we follow the thesis and use the analytic signal introduced by Gabor in 1946 [6], from which we compute the instantaneous frequency with Eq. (4.5).

    The analytic signal of a real signal \(x(t)\) is

    \[ z(t) = x(t) + i\,\mathcal{H}[x](t) = A(t)\, e^{i\theta(t)}, \]

    where \(\mathcal{H}[x]\) is the Hilbert transform of the signal,

    \[ \mathcal{H}[x](t) = \frac{1}{\pi}\, \mathrm{p.v.} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{x(\tau)}{t - \tau}\, d\tau , \]

    p.v. denotes the Cauchy principal value of the integral, \(A(t) = |z(t)|\) is the instantaneous amplitude (or envelope) and \(\theta(t) = \arg z(t)\) the instantaneous phase. The real part of \(z(t)\) is the signal itself, \(x(t) = A(t)\cos\theta(t)\). For \(x(t) = \cos(\omega t)\), the Hilbert transform is \(\sin(\omega t)\), so \(z(t) = e^{i\omega t}\) is exactly the circular motion of Section 1.

    Following Fig. 4.9 of the thesis, we take the signal \(x(t) = 0.5\sin(2\pi \cdot 10\, t) + 0.5\sin(2\pi \cdot 20\, t)\) on \([0, 1]\) seconds.

    Figure 5: (a) The signal \(x(t)\) (blue), wrapped by its envelope \(\pm A(t)\) (black). (b) The instantaneous phase of the signal, obtained from the analytic signal, in \((-\pi, \pi]\). (c) The analytic signal \(z(t)\) in the complex plane (blue): the orange segment from the origin is \(z(t)\) at a time where the instantaneous phase is close to \(\pi/6\); its length is the instantaneous amplitude, its angle with the horizontal axis the instantaneous phase, and its projections on the two axes are \(x(t)\) and \(\mathcal{H}[x](t)\).

    As time goes on, the segment traces the closed blue curve. The instantaneous phase is the angle of the segment, so it is meaningful when the curve turns around the origin.

    When are the instantaneous phase and frequency meaningful?¶

    Two properties of the analytic signal matter in practice [7, 8].

    1. The mean of the signal. The Hilbert transform of a constant is zero, so a signal with a mean \(\mu\) gives an analytic signal shifted by \(\mu\) along the real axis. If the offset is large compared with the oscillation, as for the logistic map with values in \([0, 1]\), the curve no longer turns around the origin, and the phase stays close to zero. Two signals that share nothing then look phase-synchronised. This is why hilbert_phases subtracts the mean of each node first (demean=True).
    2. The width of the spectrum. The instantaneous frequency has a clear meaning for signals whose power is concentrated around one frequency (narrow-band signals). For broadband signals, such as the chaotic logistic map in Fig. 4(d), the curve of the analytic signal makes small loops that do not contain the origin, and the phase runs backwards there: the instantaneous frequency becomes negative, which has no physical meaning.

    We check both on two uncoupled logistic maps at \(r = 4\) and on the \(x\) variable of the chaotic Rössler oscillator of Section 6, whose orbit turns around a centre.

    demean=False: phase synchronisation of two uncoupled maps = 0.489, phase runs backwards at 37% of the steps
demean=True : phase synchronisation of two uncoupled maps = 0.012, phase runs backwards at 17% of the steps

    Without subtracting the mean, two logistic maps that are not coupled at all look partly phase-synchronised, which is an artefact of their common mean of about 0.5; after subtracting it, their phase synchronisation drops to almost zero. Even then, the phase of the chaotic map runs backwards at many steps, because its spectrum is broad: its Hilbert phase measures the dependence between signals, but it should not be read as the phase of an oscillator. For the Rössler oscillator of Section 6, the phase never runs backwards.

    5. Complete Synchronisation¶

    Synchronisation is a natural phenomenon, from the pendulum clocks of Huygens in the 17th century to the fireflies that flash together [1, 3]. That chaotic systems, which are sensitive to their initial conditions, can synchronise may seem surprising, but it occurs in several forms [2]. The simplest is complete synchronisation (CS): two signals \(x_t\) and \(y_t\) are completely synchronised if

    \[ \lim_{t \to \infty} |x_t - y_t| = 0 . \]

    Following Section 4.2.3 of the thesis, we couple 5 logistic maps with \(r = 4\) on the network of Fig. 6(a), with coupling strength \(\alpha = 0.2\), and record \(10^5\) iterations after a transient of \(10^4\). Nodes 1 and 3 have the same single neighbour, node 2, so they receive the same input at every iteration.

    Maximum Lyapunov exponent: 0.372
|x1 - x3| is exactly 0 from iteration 46471 on: True

    Figure 6: (a) The network of 5 nodes, with links 1–2, 2–3, 2–4 and 4–5. (b) The cumulative absolute difference between the logistic maps of several pairs of nodes: the curve of the pair 1–3 becomes flat once the two nodes are completely synchronised, while the others keep growing. (c) The absolute difference between nodes 1 and 3 on a logarithmic scale; after the red dashed line it is exactly zero, which cannot be drawn on a logarithmic scale.

    The dynamics is chaotic, with a positive maximum Lyapunov exponent, and yet nodes 1 and 3 become identical, as in Fig. 4.4 of the thesis. When the difference becomes small enough, the two nodes, which receive the same input from node 2, end up with exactly the same value in the computer, and from then on they move as one. In the thesis, this happens around iteration \(6 \times 10^4\); the exact iteration depends on the initial conditions. As we see in the next guide, such a pair looks strongly related to any similarity measure, although the two nodes are not linked.

    6. Phase Synchronisation¶

    When the coupling is weak, chaotic oscillators can synchronise their phases while their amplitudes stay uncorrelated [11]. Two signals with phases \(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\) are phase-synchronised if the difference

    \[ \psi_{m,n} = m\phi_1 - n\phi_2 \]

    stays bounded for some positive integers \(m\) and \(n\) (Definition 4.3.1 of the thesis); here we take \(m = n = 1\). If the phase difference stays bounded most of the time but jumps by about \(2\pi\) now and then, the phases slip, which is called imperfect phase synchronisation (IPS) [2].

    Following Section 4.3.4 of the thesis, we couple 5 Rössler oscillators on the same network,

    \[ \begin{aligned} \dot{x}_i &= -\omega_i y_i - z_i + K \sum_{j=1}^{M} A_{ij}(x_j - x_i), \\ \dot{y}_i &= \omega_i x_i + a y_i, \\ \dot{z}_i &= f + z_i (x_i - c), \end{aligned} \]

    with \(a = 0.15\), \(f = 0.2\), \(c = 10\) and a small coupling strength, \(K = 0.02\). The oscillators are not identical: their frequencies \(\omega_i\) are spread evenly in \([1 - 0.015, 1 + 0.015]\). We integrate the system with RK4 and step \(h = 0.1\), drop the first \(5000\) steps and record \(10^5\) points (\(t_f = 10^4\)), together with the Lyapunov spectrum. We compute the phases of the \(x\) variables with the Hilbert transform.

    Maximum Lyapunov exponent: 0.0770
Phase runs backwards at 0.0% of the steps

    Figure 7: The absolute phase difference \(|\phi_i - \phi_j|\) between pairs of Rössler oscillators over time. (a) The pairs 1–2, 1–3, 2–3 and 4–5, whose phase difference stays bounded: they are phase-synchronised, and the pair 4–5 shows a few slips of about \(2\pi\), i.e. imperfect phase synchronisation. (b) The other pairs, whose phase difference grows steadily: their phases are not synchronised.

    The maximum Lyapunov exponent is positive, so the dynamics is chaotic (the thesis reports 0.0765), and yet nodes 1, 2 and 3 oscillate in step, as do nodes 4 and 5, as in Fig. 4.10 of the thesis. Note that the pair 1–3 is not linked: its phases lock through the common neighbour, node 2. The two groups are linked through 2–4, but their phases drift apart, because the coupling is too weak to overcome the difference of their natural frequencies.

    7. Measuring Synchronisation¶

    Plotting the differences between all pairs becomes impractical for large networks, so we use measures that summarise synchronisation in a single number.

    Amplitude order. Following Rubido et al. [12], the order parameter of a network of \(N\) nodes is

    \[ R = \frac{\left[\langle X^2\rangle - \langle X\rangle^2\right]}{\left[\langle x_i^2\rangle - \langle x_i\rangle^2\right]}, \]

    where \(X_n = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_n^{(i)}\) is the network average at iteration \(n\), \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) denotes the average over time and \([\cdot]\) the average over the nodes (Eq. (4.13) of the thesis): the variance of the network average divided by the average variance of the nodes. For complete synchrony, \(X = x_i\) and \(R = 1\), while for \(N\) independent nodes \(R \approx 1/N\). Applied to a pair of nodes (\(N = 2\)), it measures their pairwise amplitude order, which is about 0.5 for independent nodes. In the library this is cnd.global_order.

    Kuramoto phase order. For the phases \(\theta_j(t)\) of \(N\) oscillators, the Kuramoto order parameter [13] is

    \[ \rho(t) = \left| \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} e^{i\theta_j(t)} \right| , \]

    which is 1 when all phases are equal and close to 0 when they are spread around the circle (Eq. (4.14) of the thesis; there, the sum is divided by \(e^{i\Psi}\), where \(\Psi\) is the phase of the mean field, \(\arg\big(\frac{1}{N}\sum_j e^{i\theta_j}\big)\), which does not change the modulus). cnd.global_sync returns its running average over time.

    Pairwise phase order. Following Gómez-Gardeñes et al. [14], the phase order of the pair of nodes \(i\) and \(j\) is

    \[ C_{ij} = \left| \frac{1}{\Delta t}\int_{\tau}^{\tau + \Delta t} e^{i[\theta_i(t) - \theta_j(t)]}\, dt \right| , \]

    where \(\Delta t\) is the whole duration of the signal (Eq. (4.15) of the thesis). \(C_{ij} = 1\) for phase-locked nodes and close to 0 for independent ones. In the library this is cnd.pairwise_sync.

    We apply the amplitude order to the logistic maps of Section 5 and the phase orders to the Rössler oscillators of Section 6.

    Amplitude order of all 5 logistic maps: R = 0.45
Kuramoto order of the Rössler oscillators: rho = 0.49

    Figure 8: (a) The amplitude order \(R\) of the 5 coupled logistic maps of Section 5, computed from the first \(n\) iterations, as a function of \(n\). (b) The pairwise amplitude order of every pair of logistic maps, computed from the whole signal; the pair 1–3, which completely synchronises, has the highest value. (c) The running average of the Kuramoto order parameter \(\rho\) of the 5 Rössler oscillators of Section 6. (d) The pairwise phase order \(C_{ij}\) of every pair of Rössler oscillators.

    The amplitude order of the whole network stays well below 1 (about 0.4 in the thesis), which shows that the network as a whole is not coherent, although the pairwise amplitude order reveals the completely synchronised pair 1–3. In the same way, the Kuramoto order parameter of the Rössler oscillators stays far from 1 (about 0.3 in the thesis, and about 0.5 in our realisation), because the two groups of nodes drift apart, while the pairwise phase order separates the phase-synchronised pairs 1–2, 1–3, 2–3 and 4–5, with values close to 1, from the others. A single global measure can hide the synchronisation of a few pairs; this matters for network inference, because synchronised pairs, linked or not, look strongly related.

    Summary¶

    • The amplitude, the phase and the frequency of a sine wave come from circular motion, and the frequency is the rate of change of the phase divided by \(2\pi\), \(f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{dt}\).
    • The Fourier transform finds the dominant frequencies of a signal, even in strong noise, but not how they change in time; the spectrogram, the FT in a sliding window, shows that change. A chaotic signal has no dominant frequency.
    • The analytic signal \(z(t) = x(t) + i\mathcal{H}[x](t)\) of Gabor gives the instantaneous amplitude, phase and frequency of any signal. They are meaningful when the analytic signal turns around the origin: we subtract the mean of each signal first, and for broadband signals, such as chaotic maps, the phase can run backwards.
    • Chaotic systems can synchronise completely, as two logistic maps with the same input do, or only in phase, as weakly coupled Rössler oscillators do, sometimes with slips (imperfect phase synchronisation).
    • The amplitude order \(R\), the Kuramoto order \(\rho\) and the pairwise phase order \(C_{ij}\) quantify synchronisation; the pairwise measures reveal synchronised pairs that the global ones hide.

    In the next guide, we move from synchronisation to measures of dependence between signals, correlation and mutual information, which are the basis of network inference. The instantaneous amplitude and phase of this guide return in the APMSD method, whose surrogates randomise them.
